newsitem.title: CANADA: Plugged In: Something new but not necessarily for you.
newsitem.headline: Plugged In: Something new but not necessarily for you.

text.p: The Silicon Valleys of the world have entertained us for years pumping out new products on the leading edge.
Invariably these products arrive with great fanfare, then follow the path of an instant hit or the well-traveled road of marketplace oblivion.

After all it was the computer industry that brought us the 3DO game player, the Newton digital assistant and of course the Sony Mini-Disk. Where are they now? -- in various stages of remission or revival; depending on your perspective.
But Apple PowerBooks, Windows, Web Pages and Nintendo game machines are products that have been evolving for some time.
It is hard to say what makes a product take off or what makes others perform painful commercial bellyflops.

A common theme about new high-tech products is that they do not always work as advertised. One cannot forget all the early complaints about the Newton and its failure to recognize an owner's handwriting quickly.

It seems people are far more forgiving when it comes to so-called high technology, often keeping products, such as PCs or software, that perform only a portion of advertised features. It is doubtful people would stand for televisions that could not display all of its programmed channels or a music CD that played only 90 percent of its tracks.
Consider three products recently brought to the market place: IBM's Aptiva S series computer, the Timex Data Link watch and Nintendo's Nintendo 64 game player.
The Aptiva Stealth series with its slick black design and integrated speakers and graphics is an impressive unit seemingly bristling with power and possiblities.
PC Magazine (http://www.pcmag.com) heaped praise on the unit despite what it called "complicated cabling." But it loved its thumping sound.
"With stereo and its own 3D surround-sound effects, it produces loud, distortion-free video," the magazine said.

Despite its hefty price tag of more than $3,000, it sometimes behaved like most other PCs: it did things that it should not. Loading a non-Windows game on the Aptiva was still an uncertain process, which likely had more to do with with the old DOS technology than with the Aptiva.

The Timex Data Link watch is a Dick Tracy-like device that tells the time, beeps constantly and stores information such as phone numbers and personal schedules. Information is loaded via a Microsoft program on the PC and downloaded by holding the watch up to a computer screen.

Besides the snickers from office mates when you hold a beeping watch up to a monitor, it can be difficult to download the data to the watch. Sometimes the process must be repeated several times before everything cottons on.

A review on something called Gadget Boy (http://www.gadgetboy.com) on the Internet also found it wanting: "The Data Link, although fantastic for what it does, isn't complex or flexible enough to do everything a calendar book, PDA (personal digital assistant) or laptop can do."
The Nintendo 64, one of the hottest products of the past Christmas selling season, won high praise from Wired Magazine and other reviewers.

It is hard to argue with them. With each unit costing a few hundred dollars, the system, powered by a 64-bit RISC chip, seems to run unfailingly. You put in a game in, yank it out and it always seems to work. It is really plug and play. Nintendo disclosed recently that it sold four million of the players in 1996, since being launched in Japan last June and in North America in September.
The popularity of the machine can be also be seen by the dozens of Web sites on the Internet devoted to Nintendo 64, which include game reviews and discussions on future game software.
Hmmm -- a machine that is inexpensive, powerful and does not leave you scratching your head when you try to load something. Ever considered the PC business Nintendo?
